england.professionals: Solicitor, licensed conveyancer or CILEx practitioner
england.answer: In England, you are legally bound to buy only at exchange of contracts; until then an offer is not binding on either side. A solicitor, licensed conveyancer or CILEx practitioner does the legal work, and the change of ownership is registered with HM Land Registry.

sources.title: Buying a home: Transferring ownership (conveyancing) (GOV.UK)
How to buy a home (MHCLG guide, 2019, GOV.UK)
HM Land Registry registration services fees (GOV.UK)

scotland.binding_point: Concluded missives (the concluding missive is a binding contract)
scotland.professionals: Solicitor (sends the offer, handles missives, title checks and settlement)
scotland.answer: In Scotland, there is no exchange of contracts: the contract becomes binding when the missives are concluded, and the offer must be sent as a letter from your solicitor. A solicitor handles the whole legal process, and ownership is recorded in the Land Register.

sources.title: Missives (mygov.scot)
Conveyancing (mygov.scot)
Settlement (mygov.scot)

wales.professionals: Solicitor, licensed conveyancer or CILEx practitioner
wales.answer: In Wales, as in England, you are legally bound to buy only at exchange of contracts. The guides say the process and the choice of solicitor, licensed conveyancer or CILEx practitioner are the same as in England; Wales has its own Land Transaction Tax.
wales.note: Registry inferred from the England-and-Wales sequence in the England guide; no Wales-specific registry page.

sources.title: Buying a home: Transferring ownership (conveyancing) (GOV.UK)

How to buy a home (GOV.UK)

northern-ireland.professionals: Solicitor (regulated by the Law Society of Northern Ireland)
northern-ireland.registry: Land Registry (and Registry of Deeds for unregistered land), run by Land & Property Services
northern-ireland.answer: In Northern Ireland, nidirect says the sale becomes legally binding at exchange of contracts, with a deposit of at least five per cent usually paid then. A solicitor does the legal work, and ownership is recorded in the Land Registry or, for unregistered land, the Registry of Deeds.

sources.title: Buying a home - step-by-step guide (nidirect)
Consumer guide to buying and selling residential property (Law Society of Northern Ireland)
Solicitors guide to Compulsory First Registration (Department of Finance)

england.letting_minimum: E (cannot let below E without a registered exemption; £3,500 improvement cost cap)
england.answer: In England, you need an energy performance certificate before you market a property to sell or rent, and it is valid for 10 years. A landlord generally cannot let a home rated below E without a registered exemption.

sources.title: Energy Performance Certificates for buildings: selling or renting (GOV.UK)
Domestic private rented property: minimum energy efficiency standard, landlord guidance (GOV.UK, updated 5 May 2026)

scotland.answer: In Scotland, the EPC is the energy report inside the Home Report, must be provided to the purchaser free of charge, and its rating must appear in the property advertisement. Even where no Home Report is needed, the seller must provide an EPC.
scotland.note: 10-year validity is stated generally in the guide, not in the Scotland section; letting minimum not stated (guide says check gov.scot).

sources.title: Energy Performance Certificates: buildings for sale (gov.scot)
Home report (mygov.scot)

wales.letting_minimum: E (rented homes; civil penalty up to £5,000 unless exempt)
wales.answer: In Wales, rented properties must normally have an EPC rating of E or above, with a civil penalty up to £5,000 unless an exemption applies, according to Rent Smart Wales. An EPC lasts 10 years.
wales.note: Sale requirement shown as 'Yes (check the Welsh Government)' in the guide; no Welsh sale page was read.

sources.title: Energy efficiency regulations for rented homes (Rent Smart Wales)
Domestic private rented property: minimum energy efficiency standard, landlord guidance (GOV.UK, updated 5 May 2026)

northern-ireland.answer: In Northern Ireland, nidirect says an EPC is needed whenever a property is built or marketed for sale or rent, and each EPC is valid for 10 years. District councils enforce it, and the page does not mention a minimum rating for rented homes.
northern-ireland.note: Letting minimum not stated on the nidirect page read.

sources.title: Energy performance certificates (nidirect)

england.conditions: never owned a residential property anywhere in the world; intend to occupy as main residence; price £500,000 or less; relief claimed in the SDLT return
england.answer: In England, first-time buyers pay 0% Stamp Duty Land Tax on the first £300,000 and 5% on the slice from £300,001 to £500,000, with no relief above £500,000. The buyer must never have owned residential property anywhere in the world and must intend to live in the home as a main residence.

sources.title: Stamp Duty Land Tax: Residential property rates (GOV.UK)
Stamp Duty Land Tax: relief for first time buyers (GOV.UK)
SDLTM29845 - Definition of a first-time buyer (HMRC manual)

scotland.conditions: never owned a residential property anywhere in the world; intend to occupy as only or main residence; not part of linked transactions; Additional Dwelling Supplement does not apply; every joint buyer must qualify
scotland.answer: In Scotland, first-time buyer relief raises the LBTT nil rate band from £145,000 to £175,000, which cuts the tax by up to £600. The buyer must never have owned residential property anywhere in the world, must intend to live in the home as their only or main residence, and the Additional Dwelling Supplement must not apply.
scotland.note: No price limit stated in the guidance the guide read.

sources.title: LBTT3048 - First-time buyer relief (Revenue Scotland)
Residential property: LBTT rates and first-time buyer relief (Revenue Scotland)

wales.answer: In Wales there is no first-time buyers' relief, according to the Welsh Government. A first-time buyer pays the standard Land Transaction Tax rates, which start at 0% up to £225,000.
wales.note: No relief, so no threshold or price cap.

sources.title: Land Transaction Tax: guide, no first-time buyers' relief in Wales (gov.wales)
Land Transaction Tax: overview (gov.wales)

northern-ireland.conditions: never owned a residential property anywhere in the world; intend to occupy as main residence; price £500,000 or less; relief claimed in the SDLT return
northern-ireland.answer: In Northern Ireland, first-time buyers pay 0% Stamp Duty Land Tax on the first £300,000 and 5% on the slice from £300,001 to £500,000, with no relief above £500,000. The buyer must never have owned residential property anywhere in the world and must intend to live in the home as a main residence.
northern-ireland.note: Northern Ireland shares the SDLT relief with England (guide treats them together).

sources.title: Stamp Duty Land Tax: Residential property rates (GOV.UK)
Stamp Duty Land Tax: relief for first time buyers (GOV.UK)
SDLTM29845 - Definition of a first-time buyer (HMRC manual)

england.what: No seller survey; the buyer should consider a RICS Level 1, 2 or 3 survey (a lender's mortgage valuation is not a survey)
england.answer: In England, the seller does not have to provide a survey. The buyer is advised to consider an RICS Home Survey at Level 1, 2 or 3, and a lender's mortgage valuation is not the same thing as a survey.
england.note: Guide says no equivalent of the Scottish Home Report in the sources read; not stated as an explicit English rule.

sources.title: House surveys: the costs, types and benefits of one (RICS)
How to buy a home (GOV.UK)

scotland.what: Home Report: single survey and valuation (visual inspection by a chartered surveyor), property questionnaire and energy report; must be supplied within nine days of a request
scotland.answer: In Scotland, a home for sale normally comes with a Home Report made of a single survey and valuation, a property questionnaire and an energy report. The seller or agent must give it within nine days of a request, except for exempt homes such as off-plan new builds and seasonal holiday homes.

sources.title: Home Report (mygov.scot)
Housing (Scotland) Act 2006, Part 3 (legislation.gov.uk)
Property inspection technical guidance for completing Single Surveys (RICS Scotland)

wales.what: No seller survey; the buyer should consider a RICS Level 1, 2 or 3 survey (a lender's mortgage valuation is not a survey)
wales.answer: In Wales, the guides read describe no seller-provided survey; the Home Report exists in Scotland only. A buyer can commission an RICS Home Survey at Level 1, 2 or 3, which differs from a lender's valuation.
wales.note: Wales not discussed separately; 'no' rests on the guide saying England, Wales and Northern Ireland have no equivalent requirement in the sources read.

sources.title: House surveys: the costs, types and benefits of one (RICS)
How to buy a home (GOV.UK)

northern-ireland.what: No seller survey; nidirect lists getting the property surveyed as a buyer step, and the lender may require a valuation
northern-ireland.answer: In Northern Ireland, the seller does not have to provide a survey in the guides read. nidirect lists getting the property surveyed as a step for the buyer, and the lender may also need a valuation.
northern-ireland.note: 'No' rests on the guide saying there is no equivalent requirement in the sources read; the guide gives no NI-specific survey levels.

sources.title: Buying a home - step-by-step guide (nidirect)
House surveys: the costs, types and benefits of one (RICS)

england.basis: Valuation band A to H based on estimated open-market value, times the council's charge for the band, less discounts (25% if living alone)
england.answer: In England, the local property tax is council tax, set by the home's valuation band (A to H), the council's charge for that band and any discount. Bands rest on values at 1 April 1991.

sources.title: Understand how Council Tax bands are assessed (GOV.UK)
Council Tax (GOV.UK)

scotland.basis: Valuation band A to H (value ranges from section 74 of the Local Government Finance Act 1992), assessed by the local assessor, times the council's charge, less discounts
scotland.answer: In Scotland, the local property tax is council tax, with bands A to H assessed by the local assessor. The band value ranges, from £27,000 or less for A to above £212,000 for H, come from section 74 of the Local Government Finance Act 1992.
scotland.note: Valuation date not stated in the guide for Scotland.

sources.title: Local Government Finance Act 1992, section 74 (legislation.gov.uk)
Understand how Council Tax bands are assessed (GOV.UK)
Council tax high-value property bands: rates consultation (gov.scot)

wales.basis: Valuation band A to I based on estimated open-market value, times the council's charge for the band, less discounts
wales.answer: In Wales, the local property tax is council tax, with bands A to I based on values at 1 April 2003. The Welsh Government says reform, including revaluation every five years, will come in 2028.

sources.title: Understand how Council Tax bands are assessed (GOV.UK)
Find out about how we are reforming Council Tax (gov.wales)

northern-ireland.basis: Capital value times (regional rate plus district rate); value above £400,000 ignored; regional rate 0.005559 per £1 in 2026-27
northern-ireland.answer: Northern Ireland has no council tax; homes pay domestic rates, equal to capital value at 1 January 2005 times the regional rate plus the council's district rate. Value above £400,000 is ignored, and the 2026-27 regional rate is 0.005559 per £1.

sources.title: How rate bills are calculated (nidirect)
Rate poundages 2026-27 (Department of Finance)

england.answer: In England, the purchase tax is Stamp Duty Land Tax (SDLT), collected by HMRC: on a £300,000 home it comes to £5,000 for a home mover, £0 for a first-time buyer and £20,000 for an additional property.

sources.title: GOV.UK, Stamp Duty Land Tax: residential property rates (HMRC); Higher rates of Stamp Duty Land Tax (HMRC, last updated 1 April 2025)

scotland.first_time: nil-rate band raised to £175,000 (saving up to £600)
scotland.additional: Additional Dwelling Supplement, 8% of the price
scotland.answer: In Scotland, the purchase tax is Land and Buildings Transaction Tax (LBTT), collected by Revenue Scotland: on a £300,000 home it comes to £4,600 for a home mover, £4,000 for a first-time buyer and £28,600 for an additional property.

sources.title: Revenue Scotland, LBTT residential property (rates and bands as of 1 April 2021, first-time buyer relief); Scottish Budget 2025-2026: ADS rate 8% for contracts on or after 5 December 2024

wales.answer: In Wales, the purchase tax is Land Transaction Tax (LTT), collected by Welsh Revenue Authority: on a £300,000 home it comes to £4,500 for a home mover, £4,500 for a first-time buyer and £19,950 for an additional property.

sources.title: Welsh Government, Land Transaction Tax rates and bands (main residential rates from 10 October 2022, higher residential rates from 11 December 2024)

northern-ireland.answer: In Northern Ireland, the purchase tax is Stamp Duty Land Tax (SDLT), collected by HMRC: on a £300,000 home it comes to £5,000 for a home mover, £0 for a first-time buyer and £20,000 for an additional property.
northern-ireland.note: Northern Ireland applies the same SDLT as England.

sources.title: GOV.UK, Stamp Duty Land Tax: residential property rates (HMRC); Higher rates of Stamp Duty Land Tax (HMRC, last updated 1 April 2025)

england.protection_deadline: 30 days from the landlord or agent receiving the deposit
england.cap: 5 weeks' rent (annual rent under £50,000); 6 weeks' (£50,000 to £100,000)
england.penalty: County court can order a penalty of not less than the deposit and not more than 3 times the deposit, or order it repaid or paid into a scheme
england.answer: In England, a landlord must protect a tenancy deposit in an approved scheme within 30 days of receiving it. The deposit is capped at 5 weeks' rent (6 weeks' if annual rent is £50,000 to £100,000), and a county court can order a penalty of 1 to 3 times the deposit if it is not protected.

sources.title: Tenancy deposit protection (GOV.UK)
Housing Act 2004, section 214 (legislation.gov.uk)
Tenant Fees Act 2019: guidance for tenants (GOV.UK)

scotland.protection_deadline: 30 working days from the start of the tenancy
scotland.penalty: First-tier Tribunal can order up to 3 times the deposit (application during the tenancy or up to 3 months after it ends)
scotland.answer: In Scotland, a landlord must protect the deposit in one of three approved schemes within 30 working days of the tenancy starting. The First-tier Tribunal can order the landlord to pay up to 3 times the deposit.
scotland.note: Deposit cap not found in the guide's sources.

sources.title: When you must protect a tenancy deposit (mygov.scot)
When your tenancy deposit must be protected (mygov.scot)

wales.protection_deadline: 30 days (the landlord has 30 days to give the contract-holder the scheme name and repayment information)
wales.penalty: Court can order the deposit returned and award compensation
wales.answer: In Wales, under an occupation contract the deposit must go into an approved scheme and the landlord has 30 days to give the contract-holder the scheme details. A court can order the deposit returned and award compensation if it was not properly protected.
wales.note: Cap not found in the Welsh pages read. The guide's table gives 30 days to protect, while its Wales text only states 30 days to give scheme details.

sources.title: Deposits: guidance for tenants (gov.wales)
Standard occupation contracts: guidance (gov.wales)

northern-ireland.protection_deadline: 28 days from receipt (written information within 35 days)
northern-ireland.penalty: Council can fine 3 times the deposit; a court up to £20,000
northern-ireland.answer: In Northern Ireland, a landlord cannot ask for more than one month's rent as a deposit and must protect it within 28 days, giving written information within 35 days. A council can fine a landlord three times the deposit and a court up to £20,000.

sources.title: Tenancy Deposit Scheme: information for tenants (nidirect)
Private rent and tenancies (nidirect)

england.tenancy_type: Assured periodic tenancy (no end date) since 1 May 2026
england.landlord_notice: Section 8 notice with a legal ground; usually 4 months, shorter for some grounds (e.g. 4 weeks for mandatory rent arrears of at least three months)
england.answer: In England, since 1 May 2026 most private tenancies are assured periodic tenancies with no end date, and section 21 no-fault evictions are no longer available. A landlord must use section 8 and a legal ground, with notice usually of 4 months.

sources.title: Guide to the Renters' Rights Act (GOV.UK)
Renters' Rights Act overview for tenants (GOV.UK)
Private renting: tenancy types (GOV.UK)

scotland.landlord_notice: Notice to leave stating one of 18 grounds; 84 days after six months' occupation, 28 days if six months or less or for some grounds; eviction order from the First-tier Tribunal needed
scotland.answer: In Scotland, a private residential tenancy has no end date and the landlord needs one of 18 eviction grounds. Notice is generally 84 days after six months' occupation, and the landlord still needs a First-tier Tribunal order if the tenant stays.

sources.title: Private residential tenancy: information for tenants (gov.scot)
Private Housing (Tenancies) (Scotland) Act 2016, section 54 (legislation.gov.uk)
Private Housing (Tenancies) (Scotland) Act 2016, section 49 (legislation.gov.uk)

wales.tenancy_type: Occupation contract (standard contract in the private sector, periodic or fixed term)
wales.landlord_notice: No-fault notice of at least 6 months, not in the first 6 months and only if the landlord met its obligations (e.g. Rent Smart Wales registration, deposit rules); at least 1 month for breach
wales.answer: In Wales, private renters hold an occupation contract, and a landlord can end a standard contract without a ground by giving at least 6 months' no-fault notice, which cannot be served in the first six months. The landlord must have met obligations such as Rent Smart Wales registration and deposit rules.
wales.note: Marked 'yes' because a no-fault notice exists, though it is conditioned (6 months, obligations met).

sources.title: Tenants: housing law has changed (Renting Homes) (gov.wales)
Standard occupation contracts: guidance (gov.wales)
Landlords: housing law has changed (Renting Homes) (gov.wales)

northern-ireland.tenancy_type: Private tenancy under the Private Tenancies Act (Northern Ireland) 2022 (fixed term; six-month tenancy period if none agreed)
northern-ireland.landlord_notice: Notice to quit: 4 weeks (tenancy up to 12 months), 8 weeks (over 12 months up to 10 years), 12 weeks (over 10 years)
northern-ireland.answer: In Northern Ireland, a landlord ends a private tenancy by notice to quit of 4 weeks (tenancy up to 12 months), 8 weeks (up to 10 years) or 12 weeks (over 10 years). The guide lists no grounds the landlord must show, and a fixed-term tenancy can end without a notice to quit.
northern-ireland.note: Guide names no tenancy-type label and never states explicitly that no ground is needed; 'yes' inferred from the notice-to-quit rules. Longer landlord periods are in the Act but not in force.

sources.title: Private rent and tenancies (nidirect)
Private Tenancies Act (Northern Ireland) 2022 (Department for Communities)
Section 11 of the Private Tenancies Act (Northern Ireland) 2022 (Department for Communities)

guides.title: Inheritance tax on a home: the £500,000 threshold

guides.title: The title register: what it shows and how to get it
guides.description: What the HM Land Registry title register shows, official copies (£11), the £7 downloads, registration fees, and the Scottish and Northern Irish registers.

guides.title: Land Transaction Tax in Wales: rates, higher rates, 30 days

guides.title: LBTT in Scotland: rates, first-time buyers, ADS, 30 days
guides.description: Scotland's Land and Buildings Transaction Tax: 0% to £145,000, then 2%, 5%, 10% and 12%. First-time buyer relief, the 8% ADS and the 30-day return.

guides.title: Leasehold and freehold: what you own, and 2024 reforms
guides.description: Freehold or leasehold in England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, ground rent rules, and which parts of the 2024 leasehold reform Act are in force.

guides.title: Lifetime ISA for a first home: rules, 25% charge, cap

guides.title: UK mortgage affordability rules: FCA checks, 4.5x limit
guides.description: How UK lenders test affordability under FCA rules (MCOB 11.6), the 1% rate-rise stress, and the Bank of England 4.5x income limit changing on 28 October 2026.

guides.title: Mortgage in principle in the UK: what to know first
guides.description: A mortgage in principle is an early lender indication, not an offer. What to prepare, how FCA income-evidence rules shape the full application, what to ask.

guides.title: Non-UK resident SDLT surcharge: the 2% and how to reclaim it

guides.title: Private residential tenancy in Scotland: your rights
guides.description: Scottish private tenancies have no end date. A landlord needs one of 18 grounds and usually 84 days' notice; rent rises once a year with 3 months' notice.

guides.title: Renting in Wales: occupation contracts explained
guides.description: Since 1 December 2022 Welsh renters hold an occupation contract. Written statement in 14 days, 6 months' no-fault notice, 2 months' notice of a rent change.

guides.title: Renting in England: the rules since 1 May 2026

guides.title: Renting in Northern Ireland: notice, rent and deposits
guides.description: In Northern Ireland a deposit is capped at one month's rent, rent can rise once a year with 3 months' notice, and notice to quit runs from 4 to 12 weeks.

guides.title: Right to rent checks in England: what landlords must do

guides.title: Costs of selling a home in the UK: agent, legal, EPC, tax

guides.title: Service charges and ground rent on a leasehold home
guides.description: Leaseholders in England and Wales pay service charges and sometimes ground rent. Consultation limits of £250 and £100, peppercorn leases since 30 June 2022.

guides.title: Shared ownership in the UK: shares, rent and who can apply

guides.title: Stamp Duty Land Tax: rates, who pays and the 14 days
guides.description: SDLT applies in England and Northern Ireland: 0% to £125,000, then 2%, 5%, 10% and 12%. Who pays, the 14-day deadline, and what differs in Scotland and Wales.

guides.title: Tenancy deposit protection in the UK, nation by nation
guides.description: A landlord must protect your deposit in an approved scheme: 30 days in England and Wales, 30 working days in Scotland, 28 days in Northern Ireland.

professions.description: Who does conveyancing in England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, which regulator to check, and what the registers allow you to copy.

professions.title: Estate agents in the UK: redress scheme and checks

professions.title: Mortgage advisers in the UK: FCA register and fees
